title: Kalshi Injunction: First IGRA Order Sets Nov. 13 and Nov. 25 Deadlines
description: A federal court barred Kalshi sports contracts on two tribes' lands. The Kalshi injunction sets map and compliance deadlines of Nov. 13 and Nov. 25.
dek: A California judge has put the Ninth Circuit's IGRA holding into an enforceable order, with dates attached for tribal maps and Kalshi's compliance report.
author: Elena Ruiz
keywords: Kalshi injunction, Blue Lake Rancheria, Chicken Ranch Rancheria, IGRA, prediction markets, tribal gaming
body_html:
A federal judge in California has granted what the plaintiffs describe as the first preliminary injunction against Kalshi under the Indian Gaming Regulatory Act, barring the prediction-market operator from offering sports event contracts on the Indian lands of two tribes while their lawsuit proceeds. The order, issued by U.S. District Judge Jacqueline Scott Corley on a Wednesday in early November 2026 and reported on November 6, turns a September appellate holding into an operational obligation with dates attached. For tribal gaming regulators and operators, the Kalshi injunction is now less a question of legal theory and more a question of maps, compliance reports and enforcement.

The plaintiffs are Blue Lake Rancheria and Chicken Ranch Rancheria of Me-Wuk Indians. Their case reached this point after a three-judge Ninth Circuit panel ruled in September 2026 that the tribes were likely to succeed on their claim that Kalshi's sports contracts, when placed from tribal land, constitute Class III gaming under IGRA, and that federal commodities law does not displace tribal authority over gambling on Indian lands. Judge Corley had denied the tribes' request for an injunction a year earlier; after the remand, she reached the opposite result. Our earlier analysis of what the remand left open flagged harm, equities and the public interest as the remaining questions. This order answers them in the tribes' favor, at least for the two plaintiffs' lands.

What the Kalshi injunction requires, and when

According to reporting on the order, Kalshi is barred from offering sports contracts on the plaintiff tribes' Indian lands for the duration of the litigation. Two near-term dates structure the compliance process. The tribes must provide Kalshi with maps identifying the affected territories by November 13. Kalshi must then submit a report on its compliance efforts by November 25. The lawsuit itself continues toward a merits resolution.

The map requirement is the practical heart of the order. An injunction that bars activity "on Indian lands" is only as enforceable as the definition of those lands is clear to the party being restrained. Kalshi had already begun blocking access to its sports contracts on three reservations in late September, a voluntary step the company took after the Ninth Circuit's ruling. The tribes dispute that the measure is effective and allege that tribal gaming officials were still able to place bets from tribal land. The court's schedule therefore does two things: it gives Kalshi a defined geography to restrict, and it creates a documented record against which the tribes can test the company's report.

Readers unfamiliar with the statutory term should note that IGRA defines Indian lands to include land within a reservation's limits, as well as land held in trust for a tribe or individual, or held subject to a restriction against alienation, over which the tribe exercises governmental power. That definition is why a map is not a trivial exercise, and why the boundary between covered and uncovered parcels can matter. Our explainer on fee and trust land covers the distinction in more detail.

Why a first injunction under IGRA matters

Prediction-market litigation has largely been fought over preemption: whether the federal Commodity Exchange Act, administered by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, displaces state gambling law. Tribes raise a different argument. Their claim is that IGRA, a federal statute of equal standing, makes Class III gaming on Indian lands lawful only when conducted under a tribal ordinance and a tribal-state compact, and that a sports contract placed from tribal land is such gaming regardless of the platform's federal registration. The Ninth Circuit accepted that framing as likely correct. Judge Corley's injunction is the first time a district court has put that reasoning into an enforceable order.

The Commodity Futures Trading Commission has taken Kalshi's side in the broader dispute, asserting exclusive federal jurisdiction and, according to the reporting, suing states over enforcement efforts. Kalshi maintains that its sports contracts are federally regulated financial instruments rather than gambling. The company's formal response to this specific injunction had not been reported at the time of publication. Any appeal would go to the Ninth Circuit, which has already addressed the likelihood-of-success question, a fact that narrows the grounds on which Kalshi could realistically challenge the order.

The injunction protects two tribes' lands. It does not, by itself, protect every tribe, and it does not resolve the preemption question that other courts are answering differently.

The limits of the ruling

It is important not to overstate what the order does. It applies to the plaintiff tribes' lands, not to Indian country generally. Other tribes with similar claims would need to bring their own actions or benefit from the precedent in their own circuits. The Ninth Circuit's holding binds district courts within that circuit, which includes California, but courts elsewhere have diverged. The Ho-Chunk Nation's case in Wisconsin proceeds on the merits, though a preliminary injunction was denied there. Appeals courts have also allowed states such as Nevada, Ohio and Tennessee to enforce their gambling laws against Kalshi, while Kalshi has won rulings in Illinois and New Jersey, and New Jersey has asked the U.S. Supreme Court to resolve the conflict. We have tracked that divide in our coverage of the circuit split and of the Ho-Chunk ruling.

The California setting adds a further wrinkle. The state has no legal sports betting, and Kalshi has offered sports contracts to Californians since January 2025. The state has not taken enforcement action against prediction markets, leaving tribes as the principal litigants defending the exclusivity that California voters granted tribal governments in 2000. For a broader view of the state's tribal market, see the California state hub.

What to watch next

Three developments will show how durable the injunction is. First, whether the November 13 maps and the November 25 compliance report are delivered on schedule and whether the tribes contest the report's adequacy. Second, whether Kalshi seeks appellate review or a stay. Third, whether other tribes file similar claims in reliance on the Ninth Circuit's holding, or whether the Supreme Court takes up the preemption question and supersedes the regional picture. Tribal leaders will also be watching federal agency guidance on geographic trading limits, which some have said could undercut localized relief.

For operators and regulators, the immediate lesson is procedural. Court-ordered exclusion zones depend on precise land descriptions, and tribes that anticipate similar litigation would be well served by confirming that their trust and reservation boundaries are documented in a form a defendant and a court can use. Our Legal Guide provides background on IGRA's classification of gaming and the compact framework that gives these claims their force.

title: California Tribes Weigh Three 2028 Sports Betting Models
description: CNIGA has floated three models for a 2028 California sports betting ballot measure while sportsbooks pledge exclusive tribal partnerships, reports say.
dek: A single tribal platform, tribal brands or co-branding: California's tribal leadership is testing structures as DraftKings and FanDuel put commitments in writing.
author: Marcus Whitehorse
keywords: 2028 California sports betting ballot measure, CNIGA, tribal sportsbook, prediction markets, tribal gaming
body_html:
California's tribal gaming leadership is weighing how a tribe-led sports betting initiative could be structured on the 2028 ballot, and the question of which commercial partners may participate has moved from theory to correspondence. According to reporting by Capitol Weekly, republished in October 2026, the California Nations Indian Gaming Association (CNIGA) sought input from commercial operators in June on three possible models, and leaders of major sportsbooks have since written to CNIGA promising to work exclusively with tribes. The 2028 California sports betting ballot measure remains in the planning stage, but the outlines of the negotiation are visible.

Three models under discussion

The Capitol Weekly account, which quotes CNIGA Chairman James Siva and Indian Gaming Association conference chairman Victor Rocha, describes three structures CNIGA put to commercial operators in June 2026: a single tribal platform, tribally branded platforms, or co-branded platforms that pair tribes with established operators. Each answers a different question about who holds the customer relationship, who carries technology risk and how revenue is divided among tribes of very different sizes.

A single tribal platform would concentrate brand, data and technology in a tribal-controlled entity, offering the clearest sovereignty story but demanding the largest upfront build and the most consensus among California's many tribal governments. Tribally branded platforms would let individual tribes or groups of tribes operate under their own names, typically using licensed technology from a vendor, which preserves local identity but fragments the user base. Co-branded platforms would place a recognizable commercial sportsbook alongside a tribal partner, trading some brand control for player acquisition and operational experience. Our analysis of platform independence in tribal sports betting examines the technology trade-offs behind such choices.

The operators' letter

The article reports that last month the leaders of DraftKings, FanDuel and other sportsbooks sent CNIGA a letter promising to work exclusively with tribes and to close their prediction market platforms once legal sports betting arrives in California. DraftKings and FanDuel said they remain committed to working with tribal groups. Kalshi did not respond to a request for comment, according to the report. The letter is a statement of intent rather than a binding contract, and its practical value will depend on what commitments appear in the final initiative language and in any operator agreements that follow.

The timing is notable. DraftKings and FanDuel launched prediction-market products in late 2025, and the Capitol Weekly piece notes that FanDuel describes its California activity as "trades" rather than sports betting. Tribal leaders have framed prediction markets as the largest threat to tribal gaming, and the operators' letter amounts to an acknowledgment that access to a California ballot coalition may require stepping back from that business.

A possible exclusion clause

Rocha told Capitol Weekly that tribes are preparing a 2028 initiative that would bar any sportsbook that partners with a prediction market. He said Caesars, Boyd and Hard Rock would benefit under such a plan. Siva described the group's focus as a tribe-led initiative and said nothing is off the table, including tribal-only sports betting. Our earlier report on the partner-exclusion concept traces how that clause could operate. The point of the mechanism is leverage: operators wanting access to California's market would have to choose between prediction markets and a tribal partnership.

Several tribes have already complicated that picture. The report says three California tribes, including the Alturas Indian Rancheria in Modoc County, have partnered with Kalshi. Siva called the decision disappointing but said he would not hold it against them. The split mirrors a national divide, covered in our piece on Kalshi partnerships and Indian country.

Lessons carried from 2022

The 2022 campaign shapes how tribal leaders talk about 2028. Proposition 26, backed by gaming tribes, would have allowed in-person sports betting at tribal casinos and racetracks. Proposition 27, backed by DraftKings and FanDuel, would have legalized online sports betting. Neither passed, and the contest was described as the most expensive ballot fight in U.S. history. Tribes regarded the result as a win because they retained control of the state market. In April 2025, DraftKings and FanDuel executives said publicly that sports betting would not happen in California without tribal cooperation, a position the new letter appears to formalize. California tribal exclusivity itself rests on Proposition 1A, approved by voters in 2000.

What remains unsettled

Much could change before 2028. The litigation over prediction markets is moving in parallel: a federal court recently enjoined Kalshi from offering sports contracts on two tribes' lands, as we reported in our coverage of the Blue Lake remand, while other courts have ruled differently, and the U.S. Supreme Court may yet be asked to decide the preemption issue. Federal regulators are also considering rule changes. A ballot measure drafted before those questions resolve will have to anticipate several outcomes.

Equally open is how revenue would be shared among California's more than a hundred federally recognized tribes, which vary widely in size and in appetite for digital wagering. The broader California picture is available in the California state hub. Readers seeking context on how sports wagering fits within the compact framework can consult the Legal Guide.

title: The Tribal Hospitality Brand Model: Hard Rock, Tejon and the Seminole Link
description: Analysis of the tribal hospitality brand model: how Seminole-owned Hard Rock is helping the Tejon Indian Tribe build a $725 million resort in California.
dek: One tribe's brand now anchors another tribe's destination resort. What that structure offers a host tribe, and what stays under its control.
author: James Kingfisher
keywords: tribal hospitality brand model, Hard Rock Tejon, Seminole Tribe, tribal casino expansion, management contracts
body_html:
When the Tejon Indian Tribe and Hard Rock International began work in October 2026 on a more than $725 million expansion of the casino at Mettler, California, the headline numbers drew most of the attention: a 406-room hotel, 900 additional slot machines and a summer 2028 target. A less discussed feature of the project is structural. Hard Rock International is owned by the Seminole Tribe of Florida, which means one sovereign tribe's hospitality brand is now helping another tribe build and operate a destination resort. This analysis of the tribal hospitality brand model looks at why that arrangement is becoming a distinctive feature of Indian gaming, and what it does and does not change for the host tribe.

The project, in numbers

According to reporting by Tribal Business News, the existing Tejon casino opened in November 2025 along the Interstate 5 corridor, less than 15 miles south of Bakersfield, with 150,000 square feet of gaming space, 2,100 slot machines and more than 60 table games. The expansion adds a hotel of 406 rooms, including 119 suites, and 900 slots, taking the floor to 3,000 machines, an increase of nearly 43 percent. The announced amenities include convention and event space with an outdoor event lawn, two pools with cabanas, a spa with 13 treatment rooms, a Council Oak Steaks & Seafood restaurant and two additional dining outlets. The property is expected to be renamed Hard Rock Hotel & Casino Tejon.

The employment figures are significant for Kern County: more than 1,500 construction jobs, 350 permanent positions, and total property employment above 1,700. Klai Juba Wald Architecture + Interiors is architect of record and PENTA Building Group is among the project partners. We covered the groundbreaking in our report on the October start and the sequencing logic in our analysis of the open-then-expand pattern.

One tribe's brand, another tribe's land

The Seminole Tribe of Florida acquired Hard Rock International in 2007, converting a music-themed hospitality brand into a tribal enterprise. For most of the following years, discussion of the Seminole Tribe centered on its Florida gaming and its compact with the state, a subject we examine in our Seminole compact analysis and in the Seminole Tribe directory profile. The Tejon project shows a second function of that ownership: the brand can be placed on another tribe's sovereign land and operated for that tribe's benefit.

From the standpoint of the Tejon Indian Tribe, the arrangement offers three things that are difficult to build alone. The first is a brand with national recognition and a loyalty program, which shortens the time needed to reach a player base. The second is operating experience at resort scale, including hotel, convention and food-and-beverage management. The third is procurement and design capability, since a branded property typically follows established standards. The trade-off, as with any management or licensing arrangement, is that a portion of the economics flows to the brand owner, and the host tribe gives up some control over design and marketing decisions.

What stays with the host tribe

Brand partnerships do not alter the legal architecture of Indian gaming. The casino remains the host tribe's enterprise, conducted on its Indian lands under its gaming ordinance and its tribal-state compact, and regulated in the first instance by the tribal gaming commission. The Indian Gaming Regulatory Act separately requires National Indian Gaming Commission review of management contracts, and it limits the compensation a manager may receive. Our explainer on IGRA management contracts sets out how that review works, and our analysis of management contract buyouts describes how tribes eventually move to full ownership. Whether the Tejon arrangement is a management contract, a license or a hybrid is not specified in the reporting we reviewed, and readers should not assume its terms.

A tribal brand on tribal land is a commercial relationship between sovereigns. The host tribe's regulatory authority, revenue entitlements and compact obligations remain its own.

Why the model is spreading

Several pressures make brand partnerships attractive in 2026. Construction costs for destination resorts have risen sharply, and the expansion costs involved, ranging from tens of millions to more than a billion dollars, make it hard for smaller or newer operators to justify unbranded projects. Competition for hotel-casino customers is intense in California, where tribal operators compete with one another and with Nevada. A recognized brand also supports financing: lenders and landlords weighing a project of this size tend to value operator track records. Our look at hotel-room-to-slot ratios compares how Tejon's plan stacks up against other recent expansions.

There may also be a tribal-solidarity consideration: a Seminole-owned brand returns earnings to a sovereign government, and a host tribe could reasonably prefer a tribal partner to a publicly traded company, though the reporting does not say how Tejon weighed this. Counterbalancing this is the fact that Hard Rock also operates sportsbook and digital businesses, and tribes with differing views on prediction markets and digital wagering must weigh partners accordingly. Indian Gaming Association conference chairman Victor Rocha told Capitol Weekly that Hard Rock, along with Caesars and Boyd, would benefit from a California ballot structure that excludes sportsbooks partnered with prediction markets, a point explored in our coverage of the 2028 initiative.

Risks and open questions

The expansion's economics will depend on factors outside any brand's control: regional demand in Kern County, labor availability, and the cost of capital through a 2028 opening. A construction horizon of roughly twenty months from the October 2026 start to the summer 2028 target leaves room for cost drift. Brand dependence carries its own concentration risk if the partner's strategy changes. And because the property is in California, its performance will be measured against a market whose exclusivity rules and revenue-sharing obligations are set by compact, as outlined on our California state hub.

For the broader industry, the Tejon project is a useful case study in how sovereign partnerships can substitute for outside capital and operating expertise. The test will come in 2028, when the completed property shows whether a tribal brand can deliver for another tribe the results that justify the shared model.

title: What Are Indian Lands Under IGRA? How the Definition Controls Tribal Gaming
description: Indian lands under IGRA decide where tribal gaming is lawful. An explainer on the statutory definition, the 1988 land rule and why maps now matter.
dek: The statute's definition of Indian lands is narrower than most people assume, and it now decides technology disputes as well as casino siting.
author: Sarah Begay
keywords: Indian lands under IGRA, Indian Gaming Regulatory Act, trust land, Class III gaming, tribal sovereignty
body_html:
Every tribal gaming question eventually returns to a place. Whether a casino may offer Class III games, whether a state may tax or regulate it, whether a court order against an online platform reaches a particular parcel, and whether a tribe can open a second facility all depend on whether the land qualifies as "Indian lands" under the Indian Gaming Regulatory Act of 1988. The phrase is a defined term in the statute, and its meaning is narrower and more technical than the everyday idea of tribal land. This explainer sets out what IGRA means by Indian lands, why the definition matters, and where disputes tend to arise.

The statutory definition of Indian lands

IGRA defines Indian lands in two parts. The first covers all lands within the limits of any Indian reservation. The second covers lands the title to which is either held in trust by the United States for the benefit of an Indian tribe or individual, or held by a tribe or individual subject to a restriction by the United States against alienation, and over which an Indian tribe exercises governmental power. The second part contains a two-step test: the land must have a qualifying federal status, and the tribe must actually exercise governmental power over it. Owning a parcel outright in the ordinary commercial sense, known as fee land, does not meet the definition unless it falls within reservation limits or has been placed in trust.

Our explainer on fee land versus trust land walks through that distinction, and our piece on land into trust and Section 20 covers how land acquired after 1988 may become eligible for gaming.

Why the definition controls gaming authority

IGRA's framework attaches to Indian lands in several ways. Class II gaming, such as bingo and games similar to bingo, is within a tribe's jurisdiction on Indian lands if the state permits such gaming for any purpose by any person and the tribe adopts an ordinance approved by the National Indian Gaming Commission. Class III gaming, which includes slot machines and banked card games, is lawful on Indian lands only if it is authorized by a tribal ordinance, located in a state that permits such gaming for any purpose, and conducted in conformance with a tribal-state compact. Both frameworks speak of gaming "on Indian lands." If the land does not qualify, IGRA's structure does not apply to it, and the tribe's activity there is governed by other law. Our guides to Class II versus Class III gaming and to the scope-of-gaming doctrine explain those categories.

The definition also determines where tribal regulators have primary responsibility. A tribal gaming commission regulates gaming on the tribe's Indian lands, the National Indian Gaming Commission supervises under IGRA, and a state's role is limited to what the compact provides. Outside Indian lands, a tribal enterprise is typically treated like any other business subject to the laws of the jurisdiction where it operates, which is why tribal commercial ventures beyond reservation boundaries face different rules, a theme in our analysis of tribal enterprises beyond Indian lands.

The after-1988 land restriction

IGRA generally prohibits gaming on land acquired in trust after October 17, 1988, with several exceptions. Those exceptions include land taken into trust as part of a settlement of a land claim, as part of the initial reservation of a tribe acknowledged through the federal process, or as part of the restoration of lands for a tribe restored to federal recognition. A further route allows gaming on off-reservation trust land when the Secretary of the Interior determines that gaming would be in the best interest of the tribe and not detrimental to the surrounding community, and the governor of the state concurs. The governor's role in that route is examined in our explainer on governor concurrence, and the restored-lands exception in our Section 20 exceptions guide.

These rules explain why many proposals turn on the eligibility of a specific parcel. A tribe may hold land in trust for housing or government services that cannot host a casino, while another parcel only a few miles away might qualify under an exception. Eligibility determinations are typically contested by neighboring tribes, local governments and state officials, and they are often litigated.

Where Indian lands now matter in new ways

The definition has recently moved from real-estate disputes into technology litigation. In a case brought by Blue Lake Rancheria and Chicken Ranch Rancheria against the prediction-market operator Kalshi, the Ninth Circuit held in September 2026 that sports event contracts placed from tribal land are likely Class III gaming under IGRA. A federal district court then enjoined Kalshi from offering sports contracts on the two tribes' Indian lands, and, according to press reports, ordered the tribes to supply maps of the affected territories by November 13. Our report on the Ninth Circuit ruling explains the holding.

The case illustrates how the statutory definition becomes operational. A bet placed on a phone is "on Indian lands" if the bettor is physically within a qualifying parcel, which means a platform seeking to comply must translate a legal definition into geographic data. Questions that arise include how to treat parcels held in trust but not within a reservation, checkerboarded areas where tribal and non-tribal ownership alternate, and lands under pending trust applications. The same location-based logic underlies tribal mobile wagering models; see our analysis of on-reservation geofenced mobile gaming.

Practical takeaways

For tribal governments, accurate and current land records are not an administrative nicety but a legal asset. Documentation of trust status, reservation boundaries and the exercise of governmental power supports gaming authority, compact negotiations and enforcement actions alike. For operators and vendors, confirming that a facility or activity sits on qualifying Indian lands is a threshold diligence step. For the public, the definition explains why two nearby properties can face entirely different legal regimes. State-by-state context is available through the tribal gaming directory, and the compact framework that sits on top of Indian lands is described in our Legal Guide.

title: Why Tribal Kalshi Rulings Diverge: California Injunction, Wisconsin Denial
description: Tribal Kalshi rulings are splitting by circuit. Analysis of why California granted an injunction, Wisconsin denied one, and what tribes should take from it.
dek: Same statute, different courts, different results: how circuit law, the record and the choice of claim shape tribal prediction-market litigation.
author: Daniel Yazzie
keywords: tribal Kalshi rulings, Ho-Chunk Nation, Blue Lake Rancheria, circuit split, prediction markets, IGRA
body_html:
Tribal plaintiffs challenging Kalshi's sports event contracts have now obtained very different results from different federal courts, and the differences are instructive. In California, a district court has enjoined Kalshi from offering sports contracts on the Indian lands of Blue Lake Rancheria and Chicken Ranch Rancheria. In Wisconsin, the Ho-Chunk Nation's claims are proceeding, but a preliminary injunction was denied. Elsewhere, appellate courts have let states enforce gambling laws against the platform, while other courts have sided with Kalshi on federal preemption. This analysis of the divergent tribal Kalshi rulings looks at why outcomes differ, and what tribal governments should take from them.

The California result: IGRA first, then equities

The Blue Lake case followed a particular sequence. A three-judge Ninth Circuit panel ruled in September 2026 that the tribes were likely to succeed on their Indian Gaming Regulatory Act claim, concluding that Kalshi's sports contracts are Class III gaming when placed on tribal land and that federal commodities law does not override tribal authority there. The panel remanded, and Judge Jacqueline Scott Corley, who had denied the injunction a year earlier, granted it. As we explained in our analysis of the remand, the appellate holding settled the likelihood-of-success factor, leaving harm, equities and the public interest for the district court. The injunction is described as the first of its kind under federal Indian gaming law.

Two features of the California posture favored the tribes. The first is binding circuit authority on the statutory question; once the Ninth Circuit characterized the contracts as Class III gaming, the district court was not free to treat the issue as open. The second is the plaintiffs' status as the owners of the lands at issue, with claims grounded in their own regulatory authority. The Ninth Circuit's reasoning is covered in our report on the Class III ruling.

The Wisconsin contrast

The Ho-Chunk Nation's case is also grounded in IGRA, yet the Wisconsin court denied preliminary relief while allowing the claims to move forward. The reporting does not set out the court's full reasoning, and we avoid speculating about it. What the contrast shows is that a favorable merits outlook does not guarantee interim relief: preliminary injunctions turn on a combination of factors, and courts in different circuits are not bound by the Ninth Circuit's view of the statute. Our coverage of the Ho-Chunk ruling and the Seventh Circuit petition follows that case in detail.

A tribe's claim can be the same in two courts and still produce different outcomes, because binding precedent differs from circuit to circuit.

The state-law track

A separate line of cases concerns whether states may enforce their own gambling laws against Kalshi. According to current reporting, the Ninth Circuit refused to overturn a ruling that allowed Nevada to enforce its gambling laws, and the Sixth Circuit allowed Ohio and Tennessee to enforce theirs. Kalshi has won rulings in Illinois and New Jersey, and New Jersey has asked the U.S. Supreme Court to resolve the conflict. In another proceeding, the Third Circuit has been reported to hold that federal law preempts state regulation of sports-related event contracts, and California tribes and the state's attorney general have filed amicus briefs urging the Supreme Court to hear the question; the NFL also filed a brief in support of review. Our analysis of the Sixth Circuit split and the tribal amicus effort explain where tribes fit in.

The distinction between the two tracks matters. State-law cases ask whether a state's gambling statute can be enforced against a federally registered exchange, which depends on the scope of federal preemption. Tribal IGRA cases ask whether a bet placed from Indian lands is Class III gaming that requires a compact. A tribe can therefore prevail under IGRA even where preemption arguments succeed against states, because the tribe's claim rests on a different federal statute. That logic is the foundation of the Ninth Circuit's holding.

What tribes should take from the divergence

First, forum and circuit matter. Tribes in the Ninth Circuit now have favorable binding authority and a template for relief, while tribes elsewhere face open questions and should expect to build the record themselves. Second, evidence of on-reservation activity matters. In the California case, the tribes alleged that tribal gaming officials could still place bets from tribal land despite Kalshi's voluntary geofencing on three reservations, the type of concrete factual showing that supports both injunctive relief and enforcement. Third, tribes are not uniform. Several have partnered with Kalshi, and the Indian Gaming Association has criticized such arrangements, a split we describe in our analysis of fracturing tribal consensus.

Fourth, the Supreme Court may ultimately supersede the patchwork. If the Court takes a preemption case, its reasoning about the relationship between the Commodity Exchange Act and state or tribal gaming law would frame every pending dispute. Until then, outcomes will keep varying with the court, the record and the relief requested.

Looking ahead

In the near term, the California injunction sets deadlines of November 13 for tribal maps and November 25 for a Kalshi compliance report, and those filings will show how workable on-reservation exclusion is in practice. Tribal leaders also remain wary of federal guidance on geographic trading limits, which could affect how localized orders operate. For a state-level view of the market where the injunction applies, see the California state hub, and for the statutory background see the Legal Guide. We will continue to track how these rulings interact as additional courts weigh in.
